## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.103235.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.103235.3.sa2)

Summary:

While selective attention is a crucial ability of human beings, previous studies on selective attention are primarily conducted in a strictly controlled context, leaving a notable gap in underlying the complexity and dynamic nature of selective attention in a naturalistic context. This issue is particularly important for classroom learning in individuals with ADHD, as selecting the target and ignoring the distractions are pretty difficult for them but are the pre-requirement of effective learning. The authors of this study have addressed this challenge using a well-motivated study. I believe the findings of this study will be a nice addition to the fields both cognitive neuroscience and educational neuroscience.

Strengths:

To achieve the purpose of setting up a naturalistic context, the authors have based their study on a novel Virtual Reality platform. This is clever as it is usually difficult to perform such a study in the real classroom. Moreover, various techniques such as brain imaging, eye-tracking and physiological measurement are combined to collect multi-level data. They found that, different from the controls, individuals with ADHD had higher neural responses to the irrelevant rather than the target sounds, reduced speech tracking of the teacher. Additionally, the power of alpha-oscillations and frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher are found to be associated with the ADHD symptoms. These results provide new insights into the mechanism of selective attention among ADHD populations.

Weaknesses:

It is worth noting that nowadays there has been some studies trying to do so in the real classroom, and thus the authors should acknowledge the difference between the virtual and real classroom context and foresee the potential future changes.

The approach of combining multi-level data owns advantage to obtain reliable results, but also raises significant difficult for the readers to understand the main results.

- An appraisal of whether the authors achieved their aims, and whether the results support their conclusions.

As expected, individuals with ADHD showed anomalous pattern of neural responses, and eye-tracking pattern, compared to the controls. But there are also some similarities between groups such as amount of time paying attention to teachers, etc. In general, their conclusions are supported.

- A discussion of the likely impact of the work on the field, and the utility of the methods and data to the community.

The findings are an extension of previous efforts in understanding selective attention in the naturalistic context. The findings of this study are particularly helpful in inspiring teacher's practice and advancing the research of educational neuroscience. This study demonstrates, again, that it is important to understand the complexity of cognitive process in the naturalistic context.

Summary:

They employed multiple neurophysiological measures, such as EEG, eye movements, and skin conductance, to investigate the mechanistic underpinnings of paying attention in class and the disruptive effects of background noise.

The results revealed that individuals with ADHD exhibited heightened sensory responses to irrelevant sounds and reduced tracking of the teacher's speech. Overall, this manuscript presented an ecologically valid paradigm for assessing neurophysiological responses in both control and ADHD groups. The analyses were comprehensive and clear, making the study potentially valuable for the application of detecting attentional deficits.

Strengths:

• The VR learning paradigm is well-designed and ecologically valid.

• The neurophysiological metrics and analyses are comprehensive, and two physiological markers are identified capable of diagnosing ADHD.

• The data shared could serve as a benchmark for future studies on attention deficits in ecologically valid scenarios.

• Several results are null results, i.e., no significant differences were found between ADHD and control populations.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The temporal response functions (TRFs) estimated in response to the teachers' speech were similar across both groups.
claims.source: The temporal response functions (TRFs) estimated in response to the teachers' speech were similar across both groups showing the typical negative peak at ~100 ms (N1), followed by a positive peak ~200 ms (P2), and the model's predictive power following the traditional mid-central topography associated with auditory responses (Figure 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TRF analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: TRFs showed the typical negative peak at ~100 ms (N1), followed by a positive peak ~200 ms (P2).
claims.source: The temporal response functions (TRFs) estimated in response to the teachers' speech were similar across both groups showing the typical negative peak at ~100 ms (N1), followed by a positive peak ~200 ms (P2), and the model's predictive power following the traditional mid-central topography associated with auditory responses (Figure 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TRF analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: No significant between-group differences were found in the predictive power of the encoding model.
claims.source: No significant between-group differences were found in the predictive power of the encoding model (averaged across electrodes), and Bayes analysis indicates moderate support for the null hypothesis [t(47) = 0.23, p = 0.814, Cohen's d = 0.067, BF10 = 0.15].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the encoding model data.

claims.claim: The AD(H)D group showed slightly lower reconstruction correlations for the teacher's speech in the decoding model.
claims.source: However, when using a decoding model, which considers all electrodes in one model, we did find slightly lower reconstruction correlations for the teacher's speech in the AD(H)D group relative to controls [t(47) = –1.948, p = 0.057, Cohen's d = –0.557, BF10 = 1.308 (weak/moderate support for H1); Figure 2C].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the decoding model data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Participants spent most of the time looking at the teacher (60.2 ± 20.9% SEM of each trial).
claims.source: Analysis of gaze-patterns showed that, as expected, participants spent most of the time looking at the teacher (60.2 ± 20.9% SEM of each trial).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data analysis.

claims.claim: There is large variability across participants in the amount of time spent looking at the teacher.
claims.source: However, we also note the large variability across participants, with some focusing almost exclusively on the teacher (near 100%) and others spending less than 40% of the trial looking at the teacher.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data analysis showing variability.

claims.claim: No significant differences were found between groups in the amount of time spent looking at the teacher.
claims.source: No significant differences were found, however BF analysis indicated that the null hypotheses was not strongly supported [Percent gaze-time at teacher: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.899, p = 0.372, Cohen's d = –0.257, BF10 = 0.397 (weak support for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.597, p = 0.553, Cohen's d = –0.170, BF10 = 0.33 (weak support for H0); Number of gaze-shifts away from teacher: Events Condition: t(47) = 1.265, p = 0.211, Cohen's d = 0.361, BF10 = 0.547 (weak support for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = 0.644, p = 0.522, Cohen's d = 0.184, BF10 = 0.338 (weak support for H0); Figure 3C].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Neural ERPs showed three prominent centro-parietal components: a negative peak around 100 ms (N1), followed by two positive peaks around 240 and 350 ms (P2 and P3).
claims.source: Visual inspection of the neural ERPs showed three prominent centro-parietal components – a negative peak around 100 ms, which corresponds to the early sensory N1; followed by two positive peaks around 240 and 350 ms, which likely corresponds to the P2 and P3 responses, respectively (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The early N1 response was significantly larger in the AD(H)D group.
claims.source: Statistical analysis comparing ERPs in the AD(H)D vs. Control groups (collapsed across both Event-types) showed that the early N1 response was significantly larger in the AD(H)D group (p < 0.05, cluster correction; Figure 4A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: No significant differences between groups were found for the later P2 response.
claims.source: However, no significant differences between groups were found for the later P2 response.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data.

claims.claim: Both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type.
claims.source: When comparing ERPs to Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds we found that both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type, with a larger N1 for the Artificial sounds and a larger P2 for the non-verbal human sounds (both p < 0.002, cluster correction; Figure 4C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The N1 was larger for Artificial sounds compared to non-verbal human sounds.
claims.source: When comparing ERPs to Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds we found that both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type, with a larger N1 for the Artificial sounds and a larger P2 for the non-verbal human sounds (both p < 0.002, cluster correction; Figure 4C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The P2 was larger for non-verbal human sounds compared to Artificial sounds.
claims.source: When comparing ERPs to Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds we found that both the N1 and the P2 were significantly modulated by Event-type, with a larger N1 for the Artificial sounds and a larger P2 for the non-verbal human sounds (both p < 0.002, cluster correction; Figure 4C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Sound-events elicited clear event-related changes in the phasic SC response, which peaked 2–3 s after the sounds.
claims.source: Sound-events elicited clear event-related changes in the phasic SC response, which peaked 2–3 s after the sounds, and took another ~1 s to return to baseline (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by skin conductance data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The event-related SC response is consistent with the well-documented orienting reflex.
claims.source: This response is consistent with the well-documented orienting reflex, elicited following salient events.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the orienting reflex and inference from the observed SC response pattern.

claims.claim: There was a significant main effect of Event-type on event-related SC, with a higher response following artificial sounds relative to non-verbal human sounds.
claims.source: A mixed ANOVA showed a significant main effects of Event-type, with a higher response following artificial sounds relative to non-verbal human sounds [F(1, 47) = 7.88, p = 0.007, η2 = 0.143], however there was no significant main effect of Group [F(1, 47) = 0.4, p = 0.53, η2 = 0.008] or interaction between them [F(1, 47) = 0.02, p = 0.87, η2 = 0.0005; Figure 5B, C].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SC data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There was no significant main effect of Group on event-related SC.
claims.source: A mixed ANOVA showed a significant main effects of Event-type, with a higher response following artificial sounds relative to non-verbal human sounds [F(1, 47) = 7.88, p = 0.007, η2 = 0.143], however there was no significant main effect of Group [F(1, 47) = 0.4, p = 0.53, η2 = 0.008] or interaction between them [F(1, 47) = 0.02, p = 0.87, η2 = 0.0005; Figure 5B, C].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SC data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Sound-events did not elicit more frequent overt gaze-shifts away from the teacher relative to control epochs.
claims.source: However, no significant differences were found, suggesting that the sound-events did not elicit more frequent overt gaze-shifts away from the teacher, relative to what might be observed when no sound-events are present [t(48) = 1.34, p = 0.18; Figure 6A].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The likelihood of performing event-related gaze-shifts was not different for the two Event-types or in the two Groups.
claims.source: We also tested whether the likelihood of performing event-related gaze-shifts was different for the two Event-types (Artificial vs. Non-verbal human sounds) or in the two Groups (AD(H)D vs. Control) but did not find any significant main effects or interactions [Group: F(47) = 0.18, p = 0.67, η2 = 0.003; Condition: F(47) = 2.25, p = 0.14, η2 = 0.045; Interaction: F(47) = 0.51, p = 0.47, η2 = 0.01; Figure 6B].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: No significant differences between groups were found in alpha-power in either the Events or Quiet condition.
claims.source: However, none of the comparisons revealed any significant differences between groups, in either frequency band (Figure 7C) [Alpha-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.656, p = 0.514, Cohen's d = –0.18, BF10=0.34 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.394, p = 0.695, Cohen's d = –0.11, BF10 = 0.30 (moderate evidence for H0); Beta-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –1.01, p = 0.315, Cohen's d = –0.29, BF10 = 0.43 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.484, p = 0.630, Cohen's d = –0.14, BF10 = 0.314 (moderate evidence for H0)].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spectral EEG data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: No significant differences between groups were found in beta-power in either the Events or Quiet condition.
claims.source: However, none of the comparisons revealed any significant differences between groups, in either frequency band (Figure 7C) [Alpha-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.656, p = 0.514, Cohen's d = –0.18, BF10=0.34 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.394, p = 0.695, Cohen's d = –0.11, BF10 = 0.30 (moderate evidence for H0); Beta-power: Events Condition: t(47) = –1.01, p = 0.315, Cohen's d = –0.29, BF10 = 0.43 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.484, p = 0.630, Cohen's d = –0.14, BF10 = 0.314 (moderate evidence for H0)].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spectral EEG data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: No significant differences between the two Groups were observed for the global tonic or phasic SC metrics in either condition.
claims.source: No significant differences between the two Groups were observed for the global tonic or phasic SC metrics, in either the Events or Quiet condition [Phasic SC (Figure 7D, E): Events Condition: t(47) = –0.003, p = 0.99, Cohen's d = –0.0009, BF10 = 0.285 (moderate evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –0.51, p = 0.61, Cohen's d = –0.146, BF10 = 0.317 (moderate evidence for H0); Tonic SC: Events Condition: t(47) = –0.85, p = 0.398, Cohen's d = –0.244, BF10 = 0.383 (weak evidence for H0); Quiet Condition: t(47) = –1.65, p = 0.104, Cohen's d = –0.476, BF10 = 0.865 (weak evidence for H0)].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SC data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: None of the pairwise correlations between neurophysiological measures were significant after correcting for multiple comparisons.
claims.source: None of the correlations were significant after correcting for multiple comparisons (fdr-correction), however three pairs did reach significance before correction (Speech-Decoding vs. ERP-P2: r = –0.33, p = 0.021; TRF-N1 vs. event-related SC: r = –0.3, p = 0.033; ERP-N1 vs. event-related SC: r = 0.29, p = 0.04).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of neurophysiological measures.

claims.claim: The omnibus logistic regression model containing all 10 measures achieved χ2 = 15.6 with an AUC of 0.807 for predicting group allocation.
claims.source: An 'omnibus' model containing all 10 measures achieved χ2 = 15.6 with an AUC of 0.807 for predicting group allocation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate logistic regression analysis.

claims.claim: The two most dominant measures in predicting group allocation were the ERP-N1 and Speech Decoding.
claims.source: We assessed the relative contribution (dominance) of each measure by comparing the AUC of the omnibus model to 10 models with a single measure held-out. Table 1 shows ΔAUC contributed by each measure, indicating that the two most dominant measures were the ERP-N1 (positive contribution) and Speech Decoding (negative contribution), which were also the only two measures whose addition to the model reduced the AIC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dominance analysis of the logistic regression model shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: ERP-N1 and Speech Decoding together contributed an AUC of 0.15 to the omnibus model.
claims.source: Together, these two measures contributed an AUC of 0.15 to the omnibus model, which corresponds to half of the model's fit (Δχ2 = 11.8, p = 0.003 relative to a model with both measures held-out).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate regression analysis.

claims.claim: The omnibus linear regression model containing all 10 measures achieved F(10, 38) = 1.48 (p = 0.18) with an R2 of 0.28 for predicting ASRS scores.
claims.source: An 'omnibus' model containing all 10 achieved F(10, 38) = 1.48 (p = 0.18) with an R2 of 0.28 for predicting ASRS scores.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate linear regression analysis.

claims.claim: The most dominant measures for predicting ASRS scores were ERP-N1, Gaze-shifts, Alpha-power, and ERP-P2.
claims.source: The most dominant measures, who contributed at least ΔR2 > 0.3 the model, were the ERP-N1 (β = 0.3), Gaze-shifts (β = 0.288), Alpha-power (β = 0.2) and ERP-P2 (β = –0.182).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dominance analysis of the linear regression model shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: A multivariate regression model containing only the four most dominant measures significantly predicted ASRS scores (R2 = 0.227, p = 0.021).
claims.source: Although the omnibus model was not significant (see above), a multivariate regression model that contained only the four most dominant measures did significantly predicted ASRS scores (R2 = 0.227, p = 0.021), and collectively contributed ΔR2 = 0.225 (p = 0.032) to the omnibus model.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate linear regression analysis.

claims.claim: Enhanced N1 responses are often associated with heightened sensory sensitivity.
claims.source: Enhanced N1 responses are often associated with heightened sensory sensitivity (Heil, 1997; Lütkenhöner and Klein, 2007), perceptual predictability (Chennu et al., 2013; Lange, 2013; Schwartze and Kotz, 2015), and may reflect a transient detector mechanism of surprising events that can potentially (though not necessarily) trigger an attention shift (Näätänen and Picton, 1987; Escera et al., 1998; Escera et al., 2003; Berti, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on N1 responses.

claims.claim: Most studies comparing auditory ERPs in individuals with and without AD(H)D using traditional paradigms have not reported differences in early-sensory components such as the N1.
claims.source: Interestingly, most studies comparing auditory ERPs in individuals with and without AD(H)D, using more traditional paradigms (e.g., oddball), typically have not reported differences in early-sensory components such as the N1, but rather sometimes find group differences for later ERP responses (Barry et al., 2003; Gumenyuk et al., 2005; Kaiser et al., 2020; Peisch et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous ERP studies in ADHD.

claims.claim: The discrepancy in N1 findings between this study and traditional paradigms is attributed to the non-ecological nature of most traditional paradigms.
claims.source: As discussed below, we attribute these discrepancies to the non-ecological nature of most traditional paradigm.
claims.evidence: This is an inference made by the authors to explain the discrepancy in findings.

claims.claim: Neural speech tracking of continuous speech is known to be modulated by attention.
claims.source: Neural speech tracking of continuous speech is known to be modulated by attention, and is reduced when speech is not attended (Ding and Simon, 2012b; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Petersen et al., 2017; Vanthornhout et al., 2019; Kaufman and Zion‐Golumbic, 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural speech tracking.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the N1 to sound-events and speech tracking of the teacher were not correlated with each other.
claims.source: Interestingly, since the magnitude of the N1 to sound-events and speech tracking of the teacher were not correlated with each other, these results do not support the notion of an inherent 'tradeoff' between paying attention to the teacher and responding to irrelevant stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationship between these measures.

claims.claim: The two groups (ADHD and Control) are clearly separable based on ASRS scores but are far from uniform in the severity of symptoms experienced.
claims.source: This is evident from inspecting the distribution of ASRS scores in the current sample, which shows that although the two groups are clearly separable from each other, they are far from uniform in the severity of symptoms experienced.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on observation of the ASRS score distribution data.

claims.claim: Higher alpha-power is associated with reduced levels of attention/arousal.
claims.source: Higher alpha-power is associated with reduced levels of attention/arousal, and is consistently found to increase in conditions of boredom, tiredness or prolonged time on tasks (Clarke et al., 2001; Dockree et al., 2007; Palva and Palva, 2007; Wöstmann et al., 2017; Boudewyn and Carter, 2018; Jin et al., 2019; Haro et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on alpha oscillations.

claims.claim: Several studies have found higher baseline alpha-power in individuals with AD(H)D versus controls.
claims.source: Several studies have also found higher baseline alpha-power in individuals with AD(H)D versus controls (Barry et al., 2003; Johnstone et al., 2013; Bozhilova et al., 2022; Michelini et al., 2022), although results are not always consistent (Loo and Makeig, 2012; Johnstone et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on alpha power in ADHD.

claims.claim: Gaze-shifts are often used as a proxy for distraction, particularly under naturalistic conditions.
claims.source: Similarly, gaze-shifts are often used as a proxy for distraction, particularly under naturalistic conditions (Marius 't Hart et al., 2009; Foulsham et al., 2011; Risko and Kingstone, 2011; Risko et al., 2012; Hoppe et al., 2018), and recent VR and real-life eye-tracking studies have found increased frequency and prolonged duration of gaze-shifts toward irrelevant locations in individuals with AD(H)D (Braga et al., 2016; Türkan et al., 2016; Vakil et al., 2019; Mauriello et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on gaze patterns and attention.

claims.claim: Recent VR and real-life eye-tracking studies have found increased frequency and prolonged duration of gaze-shifts toward irrelevant locations in individuals with AD(H)D.
claims.source: Similarly, gaze-shifts are often used as a proxy for distraction, particularly under naturalistic conditions (Marius 't Hart et al., 2009; Foulsham et al., 2011; Risko and Kingstone, 2011; Risko et al., 2012; Hoppe et al., 2018), and recent VR and real-life eye-tracking studies have found increased frequency and prolonged duration of gaze-shifts toward irrelevant locations in individuals with AD(H)D (Braga et al., 2016; Türkan et al., 2016; Vakil et al., 2019; Mauriello et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on gaze patterns in ADHD.

claims.claim: Individuals who exhibited higher alpha-power, performed more frequent gaze-shifts and had larger N1 response to background sound-events were more likely to report experiencing attentional difficulties in real life.
claims.source: The current results extend these findings to more ecological contexts and indicate that individuals who exhibited higher alpha-power, performed more frequent gaze-shifts and had larger N1 response to background sound-events in our VR classroom were more likely to report experiencing attentional difficulties in real life.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the multivariate regression analysis showing these measures predict ASRS scores.

claims.claim: No single neurophysiological measure alone is sufficient for explaining differences between individuals in attentional functioning.
claims.source: What is clear, though, is that no single neurophysiological measure alone is sufficient for explaining differences between the individuals – whether through the lens of clinical diagnosis or through report of symptoms.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the multivariate analysis results showing multiple measures contribute to explaining variance.

claims.claim: Attentional challenges may manifest in a variety of different ways, indexed through different neurophysiological responses.
claims.source: These data emphasize the complex nature of attentional functioning, especially under realistic conditions, and that fact that 'attentional challenges' may manifest in a variety of different ways, indexed though different neurophysiological responses.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that multiple uncorrelated measures contribute to explaining ADHD symptoms.

claims.claim: The P3a ERP component is typically observed at a latency of ~250–400 ms after hearing novel or surprising sounds.
claims.source: In traditional ERP studies, distractibility by irrelevant stimuli is often associated with a family of late-latency positive neural responses (the P300 family), and specifically the P3a ERP component, which is typically observed at a latency of ~250–400 ms after hearing novel or surprising sounds (SanMiguel et al., 2010; Wetzel et al., 2013; Masson and Bidet-Caulet, 2019; Barry et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the P3a component.

claims.claim: Past studies have shown reduced P3a responses in individuals with AD(H)D.
claims.source: Moreover, past studies have shown reduced P3a responses in individuals with AD(H)D (Barry et al., 2003; Gumenyuk et al., 2005; Kaiser et al., 2020; Peisch et al., 2021; Kwasa et al., 2023), leading us to expect a similar pattern here.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on P3a in ADHD.

claims.claim: The P3a is typically observed in tasks that require high levels of perceptual vigilance to discriminate between specific stimulus features.
claims.source: The P3a is typically observed in tasks that require high levels of perceptual vigilance to discriminate between specific stimulus features, such as the pitch, duration or intensity of sounds presented in an oddball paradigm.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of P3a research and the typical experimental contexts in which it is observed.

claims.claim: In oddball paradigms, 'distractor' sounds are within the focus of participants' endogenous attention rather than truly 'background' stimuli.
claims.source: Accordingly, although these 'distractor' stimuli do not require an explicit response, they are in fact within the focus of participants' endogenous attention, rather than truly 'background' stimuli (Makov et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the nature of attention in oddball paradigms, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The role of novel sound-events in the VR classroom differs substantially from their role in oddball paradigms.
claims.source: This differs substantially from the role of the novel sounds-events in the VR classroom task used here, where sound-events are clearly in the background– both spatially and semantically – and occur in parallel to an ongoing speech stimulus (the lecture) that participants are primarily paying attention to.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference comparing the current experimental design to traditional oddball paradigms.

claims.claim: Participants in both groups achieved similar behavioral performance in the Quiet and Events condition.
claims.source: Participants in both groups achieved similar behavioral performance in the Quiet and Events condition, suggesting that the presence of occasional sound-events ultimately did not ultimately impair their ability to understand the content of the mini-lectures (at least at the level probed by our comprehension questions).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data analysis showing no significant differences.

claims.claim: The task was deliberately chosen to mimic the level of information processing required in real-life learning contexts.
claims.source: These results should be interpreted bearing in mind the details of the current task design – we deliberately chose a task that would mimic the level of information processing required in real-life learning contexts as opposed to speeded-response tasks used in traditional attention research that encourage failures of performance by creating perceptually 'extreme' conditions (Hall et al., 2016; Barkley, 2019; Arrondo et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design choices made by the authors.

claims.claim: Neurophysiological indications of somewhat reduced attention do not necessarily translate to poorer behavioral outcomes.
claims.source: Under these conditions, individuals with and without AD(H)D were able to maintain good performance despite the occasional acoustic disturbances (Mandal et al., 2024), indicating that neurophysiological indication of somewhat reduced attention do not necessarily translate to poorer behavioral outcomes.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that neural differences were observed without corresponding behavioral differences.

claims.claim: The SC orienting reflex is considered obligatory and automatic.
claims.source: This response is considered obligatory and automatic, and does not require allocation of attention as it can be observed during sleep and other unconscious states (albeit the magnitude of these responses can vary as a function of attention).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the orienting reflex.

claims.claim: There has been much debate regarding the relationship between the SC orienting reflex and early neural responses.
claims.source: Indeed, there has been much debate regarding the relationship between the SC orienting reflex and early neural responses, with conflicting results reported across studies (Lim et al., 1996; MacDonald and Barry, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research showing conflicting results.

claims.claim: Peripheral auditory stimuli may be less effective than visual stimuli at capturing overt attention.
claims.source: These results might indicate that peripheral auditory stimuli are, generally, less effective than visual stimuli at capturing overt attention (Turoman and Vergauwe, 2024; Mandal et al., 2024), or that in ecological audiovisual settings individuals are less prone to move their eyes to search for the source of auditory disturbances, despite noticing them.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the null finding for gaze-shifts, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In ecological audiovisual settings individuals may be less prone to move their eyes to search for the source of auditory disturbances, despite noticing them.
claims.source: These results might indicate that peripheral auditory stimuli are, generally, less effective than visual stimuli at capturing overt attention (Turoman and Vergauwe, 2024; Mandal et al., 2024), or that in ecological audiovisual settings individuals are less prone to move their eyes to search for the source of auditory disturbances, despite noticing them.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the null finding for gaze-shifts.

claims.claim: Classification of the AD(H)D group was based on their prior clinical diagnosis.
claims.source: First, as noted, classification of the AD(H)D group was based on their prior clinical diagnosis, which likely varied across participants in terms of diagnosis approach and age of diagnosis.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: The two groups were distinguishable in their self-reported ASRS scores.
claims.source: Although the two groups were distinguishable in their self-reported ASRS scores, a more reliable assessment of the severity of current AD(H)D symptoms might have been achieved if we had conducted a full clinical assessment of all participants, as per the acceptable clinical guidelines (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ASRS data showing significant group differences.

claims.claim: This study was conducted on adults, whereas the majority of AD(H)D research has focused on children.
claims.source: Second, this study was conducted on adults, whereas the majority of AD(H)D research – and particularly all VR classroom studies – have focused on children (Pollak et al., 2009; Neguț et al., 2017; Schweitzer and Rizzo, 2022; Seesjärvi et al., 2022; Stokes et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the sample characteristics and comparison to previous research.

claims.claim: The adult cohort tested included primarily university students with relatively high cognitive and learning abilities.
claims.source: Moreover, the adult cohort tested here included primarily university students, who do not represent all adults but rather are a subgroup with relatively high cognitive and learning abilities, who are accustomed to sitting in lectures for long periods of time (Henrich et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the sample characteristics and potential limitations.

claims.claim: The lack of group differences in some metrics may be because these individuals have learned to deal with distraction and have developed appropriate strategies.
claims.source: Hence, it is possible that the lack of group differences in some metrics in the current dataset (and particularly in their behavioral outcomes) is because these individuals have learned to deal with distraction and have developed appropriate strategies, which allow them to thrive in academic settings.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about why certain null results were observed.

claims.claim: Withstanding distraction in real-life contexts may be improved through training and good habit-forming, even in individuals with AD(H)D.
claims.source: Specifically, they suggest that withstanding distraction in real-life contexts may be improved through training and good habit-forming, even in individuals with AD(H)D.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the results.

claims.claim: Individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds.
claims.source: Here, we found that both of these operations are less effective in individuals who are diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms of difficulties in everyday attention. Specifically, these individuals exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds, reduced speech tracking of the teacher, a tendency toward more frequent gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and somewhat increased alpha-power.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from ERP analysis.

claims.claim: Individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms exhibit reduced speech tracking of the teacher.
claims.source: Here, we found that both of these operations are less effective in individuals who are diagnosed with AD(H)D or who report more severe symptoms of difficulties in everyday attention. Specifically, these individuals exhibit heightened sensory response to irrelevant sounds, reduced speech tracking of the teacher, a tendency toward more frequent gaze-shifts away from the teacher, and somewhat increased alpha-power.

results.result: Participants in both ADHD and control groups achieved high comprehension accuracy (~88%) in both Events and Quiet conditions, with no significant between-group differences, indicating that occasional sound-events did not disrupt understanding of mini-lessons.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 provide converging behavioral evidence showing good performance across groups and conditions. Statistical tests with Bayes factors support the lack of group differences, though the authors acknowledge weak support for the null hypothesis.

results.result: Neural speech tracking analysis revealed similar TRF patterns across groups in the encoding model, but the ADHD group showed marginally lower reconstruction correlations in the decoding model (p=0.057), suggesting reduced speech tracking of the teacher.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 show mixed results: the encoding model found no significant differences (C30), while the decoding model showed a trend-level effect (C31, p=0.057). The marginal significance and weak/moderate Bayes factor (BF10=1.308) make this finding uncertain. The multivariate approach (C110-C111) is methodologically sound but the primary result remains at the threshold of significance.

results.result: Participants spent most time looking at the teacher (60.2%), with large inter-individual variability, but no significant between-group differences in gaze time or gaze-shifts away from the teacher.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 are supported by eye-tracking data with appropriate statistical tests. However, the authors note weak Bayes factor support for the null hypothesis, indicating the evidence is not conclusive but the data pattern is clear.

results.result: ERPs to sound-events showed three components (N1, P2, P3). The N1 was significantly larger in the ADHD group, and both N1 and P2 were modulated by event-type (larger N1 for artificial sounds, larger P2 for non-verbal human sounds), with no group differences in P2 or P3.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are well-supported by ERP data with cluster-corrected statistics and ANOVA confirmation. The N1 group difference (p<0.05) and event-type effects (p<0.002) are robust. The lack of interaction effects is properly reported.

results.result: Sound-events elicited phasic skin conductance responses peaking 2-3s post-stimulus, consistent with the orienting reflex. Artificial sounds elicited larger responses than non-verbal human sounds, but there were no group differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by SC data with appropriate ANOVA statistics. The event-type effect is significant (p=0.007), while group effects are clearly non-significant. The interpretation as orienting reflex (C42) is reasonable given established knowledge.

results.result: Sound-events did not elicit more frequent overt gaze-shifts away from the teacher compared to control epochs, with no differences between event-types or groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by statistical analysis showing null effects. This is a clear negative result with appropriate statistical testing, though it contradicts some prior literature expectations.

results.result: No significant between-group differences were found in alpha-power, beta-power, or global tonic/phasic skin conductance in either condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 report consistent null findings across multiple neurophysiological measures with appropriate statistics and Bayes factors. The moderate evidence for H0 in some comparisons strengthens confidence in these null results.

results.result: Multivariate logistic regression predicting ADHD diagnosis achieved AUC=0.807, with ERP-N1 and Speech Decoding as the two most dominant predictors, together contributing half of the model's fit.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 describe a well-executed multivariate analysis with dominance analysis. The lack of significant correlations between measures (C50) supports their independence. The logistic regression results are clearly reported with appropriate metrics (AUC, χ2, AIC).

results.result: Linear regression predicting ASRS scores identified ERP-N1, gaze-shifts, alpha-power, and ERP-P2 as dominant predictors. While the full model was non-significant (p=0.18), a reduced model with these four measures significantly predicted ASRS scores (R²=0.227, p=0.021).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 present a coherent multivariate analysis. The non-significance of the omnibus model (C54) is honestly reported, but the significant reduced model (C56) provides meaningful results. The dominance analysis (C55) appropriately identifies key predictors.

results.result: Individuals with ADHD exhibited heightened neural responses (larger N1) to irrelevant sounds and reduced speech tracking of the teacher compared to controls.
results.evaluation: The N1 finding (C3, C36, C88) is well-supported with p<0.05. However, the speech tracking reduction (C4, C31, C89) only reached trend-level significance (p=0.057) in the decoding model. The combination of one robust and one marginal finding makes the overall result uncertain.

results.result: Alpha-power and gaze-shifts away from the teacher contributed to explaining variance in self-reported ADHD symptoms, with individuals showing higher alpha-power, more gaze-shifts, and larger N1 responses more likely to report attentional difficulties.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C55 are supported by the multivariate regression analysis showing these measures as dominant predictors of ASRS scores. Claims C67, C90-C91 appropriately synthesize these findings. The reduced model (C56) significantly predicted symptoms.

results.result: The neurophysiological metrics measured were not significantly correlated with each other, suggesting they represent different manifestations of inattention/distraction rather than a general biomarker.
results.evaluation: Claims C61, C92-C93 are supported by correlation analysis (C50) showing no significant correlations after FDR correction. This finding is important for interpreting the multivariate results and supports the conceptual interpretation.

results.result: No single neurophysiological measure alone is sufficient for explaining individual differences in attentional functioning, and ADHD may not be characterized by a specific neural marker under ecological conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C94 are well-supported by the multivariate analyses showing multiple uncorrelated measures contribute to explaining variance. This is a key conceptual conclusion appropriately drawn from the data pattern.

results.result: Enhanced N1 responses are associated with heightened sensory sensitivity, and the discrepancy between this study's N1 findings and traditional paradigms is attributed to ecological differences in task context.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 provide appropriate contextualization of the N1 findings. C57 is supported by citations, C58 accurately summarizes prior literature, and C59 offers a reasonable interpretation of the discrepancy, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The absence of P3a differences between groups, contrary to traditional paradigm findings, is explained by fundamental differences in task demands and the functional status of sound-events between VR classroom and oddball paradigms.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 provide a well-reasoned explanation for the null P3a finding. The distinction between truly background stimuli in the VR classroom versus attended distractors in oddball tasks (C73-C74) is conceptually sound and supported by citations.

results.result: Despite neurophysiological differences, both groups maintained good behavioral performance, indicating that neurophysiological indications of reduced attention do not necessarily translate to poorer behavioral outcomes in ecologically valid tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 appropriately synthesize the behavioral and neural findings. The interpretation that task design matters (C76) and that neural differences don't always predict behavior (C77) is well-supported by the data pattern.

results.result: The study included 49 participants (24 ADHD, 25 controls) matched for age, with ADHD classification based on prior clinical diagnosis and validated by significantly higher ASRS scores in the ADHD group.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83, C96-C101, C103 accurately describe the sample characteristics and validation. The significant ASRS difference (p<0.001, C103) validates group allocation, though the authors acknowledge limitations of relying on prior diagnosis (C82).

results.result: The study was conducted on university students with ADHD, a high-functioning subgroup that may have developed compensatory strategies, potentially explaining some null behavioral findings and suggesting that attention skills can be improved through training.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 accurately describe sample characteristics. However, C86-C87 are speculative explanations for null findings without direct evidence. While plausible, these remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: The VR classroom was developed in Unity with 30 trials (22 Events, 8 Quiet), presenting 104 sound-events total, with neural activity recorded via 64-channel EEG at 1024 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 provide clear methodological details about the experimental setup. These are straightforward descriptive claims about the methods used.

results.result: ADHD is characterized by attention difficulties in classrooms, but traditional assessment tools lack ecological validity and fail to capture real-life attention challenges.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C13 establish the motivation for the study through general knowledge (C1, C7-C9) and citations to prior literature (C10-C13). These background claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: VR has been increasingly used in cognitive research and shows promise for ADHD assessment, but most VR classroom studies still use non-ecological tasks and rely on indirect behavioral outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 accurately summarize the state of VR research in ADHD with appropriate citations. This provides context for the current study's contribution.

results.result: The study measured multiple neurophysiological metrics previously associated with attention: neural speech tracking, ERPs, gaze-shifts, and oscillatory power, each with established links to attention processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23 establish the theoretical basis for the chosen measures through citations to prior research. These are well-supported background claims that justify the methodological choices.

results.result: Prior research has established that neural speech tracking is modulated by attention, alpha-power is associated with reduced attention/arousal, and gaze-shifts are used as proxies for distraction, with some evidence of alterations in ADHD.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C63-C66 provide appropriate literature context for interpreting the results, with citations to relevant prior work. These establish the expected patterns based on previous research.

results.result: The SC orienting reflex is considered obligatory and automatic, though there is debate about its relationship to early neural responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 accurately represent established knowledge about the orienting reflex and acknowledge ongoing debate in the literature with appropriate citations.

results.result: The lack of gaze-shifts following auditory events may indicate that peripheral auditory stimuli are less effective than visual stimuli at capturing overt attention, or that individuals are less prone to search for auditory sources in ecological settings.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are explicitly speculative ("might indicate", "may be") explanations for the null gaze-shift finding. While plausible and supported by some citations, these remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: There is a need to adopt more nuanced and dimensional approaches to defining attention-disorders and designing ecologically valid testing methods.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by citations to recent literature and represents a reasonable conclusion drawn from the study's findings about the complexity of attention measures.

results.result: The ASRS questionnaire has good psychometric properties and high sensitivity for ADHD diagnosis.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by citations to validation studies. This establishes the validity of using ASRS as an outcome measure.

results.result: The ADHD and control groups are clearly separable based on ASRS scores but show substantial within-group variability in symptom severity.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by observation of the ASRS distribution data (Figure 9) and provides important context for interpreting the dimensional analyses.

results.result: Individuals with ADHD exhibited significantly larger N1 ERP responses to irrelevant background sounds compared to controls (C3, C36), reflecting heightened sensory responses to distractors (C88).
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states 'Solid evidence is provided that individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D differ from control participants in both the encoding of the target sound and the encoding of acoustic interference.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'individuals with ADHD had higher neural responses to the irrelevant rather than the target sounds.' No concerns were raised about this result.

results.result: Individuals with ADHD showed reduced neural speech tracking of the teacher's speech in the decoding model (C4, C31), indicating less effective processing of the target speech (C89).
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'Solid evidence is provided that individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D differ from control participants in both the encoding of the target sound.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'reduced speech tracking of the teacher' as a key finding. Reviewer 1 notes the decoding result as 'clear and strong,' though acknowledges the p-value is marginal (p=0.057).

results.result: Alpha-power and gaze-shifts away from the teacher were among the dominant predictors of self-reported ADHD symptoms (ASRS scores) across the sample (C5, C6, C55, C56), with individuals showing higher alpha-power and more frequent gaze-shifts reporting more attentional difficulties (C67, C90, C91).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the power of alpha-oscillations and frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher are found to be associated with the ADHD symptoms.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges the multivariate regression analyses as 'good ideas' and finds the results 'interesting in that it informs us on which metrics are sensitive to group-effects.' No concerns were raised about these dimensional findings.

results.result: Both ADHD and control groups achieved similarly high comprehension performance (~88% accuracy) in both Events and Quiet conditions (C24, C25, C27), indicating that occasional sound-events did not disrupt overall understanding of the lessons (C26, C75).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'there are also some similarities between groups such as amount of time paying attention to teachers, etc.' and states 'their conclusions are supported.' Reviewer 4 acknowledges 'Several results are null results' but does not challenge their validity. The reviewers accept that neurophysiological differences can exist without behavioral impairment in this task context.

results.result: No significant group differences were found in gaze-time at the teacher or in event-related gaze-shifts (C34, C45, C46), suggesting that sound-events did not elicit more overt attention shifts in either group.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'some similarities between groups such as amount of time paying attention to teachers' and confirms 'their conclusions are supported.' Reviewer 4 notes 'Several results are null results' but raised no validity concerns. The authors' interpretation that overt gaze behavior may not capture all aspects of distraction is implicitly accepted.

results.result: No significant between-group differences were found in alpha-power or beta-power when comparing ADHD and control groups directly (C47, C48).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly acknowledges 'Several results are null results, i.e., no significant differences were found between ADHD and control populations' but confirms 'The authors have addressed all of my concerns.' The null finding is accepted as valid, consistent with the dimensional approach showing alpha-power predicts symptom severity rather than group membership.

results.result: No significant group differences were found in event-related or global skin conductance measures (C44, C49), indicating similar autonomic arousal responses to sound-events in both groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 notes 'Several results are null results' but confirms 'The authors have addressed all of my concerns.' No reviewer challenged the validity of these null findings. The results are consistent with the authors' interpretation that SC reflects automatic orienting rather than attentional capture.

results.result: A multivariate logistic regression model using all neurophysiological measures achieved good classification of ADHD vs. control groups (AUC=0.807), with ERP-N1 and Speech Decoding as the two most dominant predictors (C51, C52, C53).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the multivariate analyses are 'good ideas' and finds the approach 'useful in itself.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'two physiological markers are identified capable of diagnosing ADHD.' While Reviewer 1 notes the analyses 'would benefit from additional clarifications,' no fundamental concerns about validity were raised, and clarifications were apparently addressed in revision.

results.result: A multivariate linear regression model identified ERP-N1, gaze-shifts, alpha-power, and ERP-P2 as dominant predictors of ASRS symptom scores (C54, C55), with a reduced model containing only these four measures significantly predicting symptoms (R²=0.227, p=0.021) (C56).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 finds the multivariate regression analyses 'interesting in that it informs us on which metrics are sensitive to group-effects and correlated with each other.' Reviewer 3 confirms the findings provide 'new insights into the mechanism of selective attention among ADHD populations.' The dimensional approach is accepted as valid and informative.

results.result: The neurophysiological measures were largely uncorrelated with each other after multiple comparison correction (C50, C92), suggesting they represent different manifestations of inattention rather than a single biomarker (C93).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises the finding that results 'informs us on which metrics are sensitive to group-effects and correlated with each other.' The lack of strong correlations supports the authors' interpretation of multiple independent pathways to attentional difficulties, which aligns with reviewers' acceptance of the complex, multidimensional nature of ADHD.

results.result: Both N1 and P2 ERP components were modulated by event-type, with larger N1 for artificial sounds and larger P2 for non-verbal human sounds (C38, C39, C40), and skin conductance showed higher responses to artificial sounds (C43).
results.evaluation: These stimulus-type effects are reported as significant findings in the manuscript. No reviewer questioned these results or raised concerns about their validity. The effects are accepted as demonstrating sensitivity of the measures to acoustic properties of the distractors.

results.result: The temporal response functions (TRFs) to teacher speech showed typical N1 and P2 components with similar morphology across groups (C28, C29), and no significant group differences in the encoding model's predictive power (C30).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the first part of the results clear and strong' and no concerns were raised about the TRF methodology or these specific findings. The null result for the encoding model is accepted, with the decoding model providing the more sensitive measure of group differences.

results.result: No single neurophysiological measure alone is sufficient for explaining attentional differences (C68), with attentional challenges manifesting through multiple independent neurophysiological responses (C69), suggesting ADHD may not be characterized by a specific neural marker under ecological conditions (C94).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states this represents 'an interesting first step into more naturalistic measurement of speech attention' and that 'much more work is needed to clarify how these results change with different stimuli and tasks.' Reviewer 3 confirms the findings 'provide new insights into the mechanism of selective attention' and demonstrate 'the complexity of cognitive process in the naturalistic context.' The multidimensional interpretation is accepted.

results.result: Traditional attention assessment paradigms lack ecological validity and sensitivity for real-life attention challenges (C2, C12, C13), while VR approaches offer improved ecological validity (C14, C15) though most still use non-ecological tasks (C16).
results.evaluation: The editor states 'The VR paradigm here can potentially bridge lab experiments and real-life experiments.' Reviewer 3 praises the VR approach as 'clever as it is usually difficult to perform such a study in the real classroom' and confirms 'The VR learning paradigm is well-designed and ecologically valid.' The motivation for the study is fully accepted.

results.result: Speech-tracking analysis required a multivariate approach to account for variance from event-sounds (C110), with the multivariate model explaining significantly more variance than the univariate model (C111).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly discusses the hyperparameter tuning approach, stating 'In this specific case, I think the authors had a good reason to do so' and concludes 'The authors have done a great job at addressing my comments. I don't have any further concerns.' The methodological choice is accepted as appropriate for this study.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the N1 finding (C3, C36, C88) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval rates overall result as UNCERTAIN due to marginal speech tracking result (C4, C89), while peer review separates these findings and rates N1 evidence as solid and explicitly affirmed by multiple reviewers.

Both address speech tracking claims (C4, C31, C89). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to marginal p-value (0.057) and weak Bayes factor. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 calling it 'clear and strong' despite acknowledging the marginal p-value, and editor stating 'solid evidence' is provided.

Strong agreement on dimensional findings (C5, C6, C55, C67, C90, C91). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the reduced model's significance and dominance analysis. Peer review confirms findings are 'associated with ADHD symptoms' and finds the multivariate approach 'interesting' and informative.

Strong agreement on behavioral null findings (C24-C27). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes converging evidence with appropriate statistics despite weak Bayes factors. Peer review explicitly accepts that neurophysiological differences can exist without behavioral impairment in this context.

Both address gaze behavior null findings (C45, C46, C34). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes clear negative result with appropriate testing. Peer review accepts the null findings and the interpretation that overt gaze may not capture all aspects of distraction.

Both address alpha-power null findings (C47, C48). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes moderate Bayes factor evidence for H0. Peer review explicitly acknowledges null results and confirms authors addressed concerns, consistent with dimensional approach showing alpha predicts symptoms rather than group membership.

Both address SC null findings (C44, C49). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes significant event-type effect with non-significant group effects. Peer review accepts null findings as valid, consistent with interpretation that SC reflects automatic orienting rather than attentional capture.

Strong agreement on logistic regression analysis (C51, C52, C53). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes well-executed dominance analysis with appropriate metrics. Peer review calls multivariate analyses 'good ideas' and 'useful,' with clarifications addressed in revision.

Perfect agreement on multivariate regression findings (C54, C55, C56). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes honest reporting of non-significant omnibus model with meaningful reduced model. Peer review finds results 'interesting' and informative about metric sensitivity, providing 'new insights' into selective attention mechanisms.

Strong agreement on lack of correlations between measures (C50, C61, C92, C93). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes importance for interpreting multivariate results. Peer review explicitly praises finding as informing which metrics are sensitive and correlated, supporting multiple independent pathways interpretation.

Perfect agreement on multidimensional interpretation (C68, C69, C94). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes multiple uncorrelated measures contributing to variance. Peer review accepts this as 'interesting first step' into naturalistic measurement, demonstrating 'complexity of cognitive process in naturalistic context.'

Both address ERP findings (C35-C40, C38, C39, C40, C43). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes robust N1 group difference and event-type effects with cluster-corrected statistics. Peer review accepts stimulus-type effects without concerns, demonstrating measure sensitivity to acoustic properties.

Both address TRF encoding model (C28, C29, C30). OpenEval rates overall as UNCERTAIN due to mixed encoding/decoding results. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, noting 'clear and strong' results with no concerns about methodology, accepting null encoding result with decoding model providing more sensitive measure.

Both address VR research context and motivation (C14, C15, C16, C2, C12, C13). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes accurate literature summary with appropriate citations. Peer review strongly endorses VR approach as 'clever,' 'well-designed,' and 'ecologically valid,' with potential to bridge lab and real-life experiments.

Both address multivariate TRF approach (C110, C111). OpenEval rates overall result as UNCERTAIN due to marginal primary finding but notes methodological soundness. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 stating authors 'had good reason' for hyperparameter tuning approach and confirming concerns were addressed.

OpenEval evaluates eye-tracking data (C32, C33, C34) as SUPPORTED with appropriate statistics but weak Bayes factors. No corresponding focused peer review evaluation found, though C34 appears in peer R5 addressing broader gaze behavior findings.

OpenEval evaluates contextualization of N1 findings (C57, C58, C59) as SUPPORTED with reasonable interpretation of discrepancy with prior literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this interpretive discussion.

OpenEval evaluates explanation for null P3a finding (C70-C74) as SUPPORTED with well-reasoned distinction between VR classroom and oddball tasks. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this interpretive discussion.

OpenEval evaluates synthesis of behavioral and neural findings (C75, C76, C77) as SUPPORTED, noting task design matters and neural differences don't always predict behavior. Peer R4 touches on C75 but doesn't provide focused evaluation of this synthesis.

OpenEval evaluates sample characteristics and validation (C82, C83, C96-C101, C103) as SUPPORTED with significant ASRS difference validating groups. No corresponding focused peer review evaluation found for these methodological details.
